extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners evaluating patent claim eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101, with particular application to computer-implemented inventions, machine learning, and AI-related claims. Updates incorporate the precedential Ex Parte Desjardins decision and related Federal Circuit precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether claims are directed to improvement in computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claims are directed to an improvement to computer functionality versus being directed to an abstract idea, recognizing that software improvements may be logical structures and processes rather than particular physical features (Enfish)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedent like Enfish and McRO when assessing eligibility, particularly for claims related to machine learning or AI. Software can make non-abstract improvements to computer technology just as hardware can; eligibility determinations should turn on whether the claims are directed to an improvement to computer functionality versus an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate specification for disclosed technological improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should be evaluated to determine if the disclosure provides sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to other technology or a technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not explicitly set forth the improvement, but it must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to one of ordinary skill. Conversely, a conclusory bare assertion of an improvement without necessary detail is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require that the claim reflects the disclosed improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification sets forth an improvement in technology or a technical field, the claim must be evaluated to ensure that the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement — i.e., the claim includes the components or steps of the invention that provide the improvement described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim does not need to explicitly recite the improvement (e.g., “thereby increasing the bandwidth of the channel”), but examiners must verify the claim includes the components or steps that provide the improvement. Consider the claim "as a whole" and under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to determine whether the claim reflects the disclosed improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claims as an ordered combination / as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim reflects an improvement, look at the claim 'as a whole' — in other words, evaluate the claim as an ordered combination without ignoring the requirements of the individual steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to avoid oversimplifying the claims by looking at them generally and failing to account for the specific requirements of the claims. Do not evaluate claims at an inappropriately high level of generality such that meaningful technical limitations are dismissed without adequate explanation (see Ex Parte Desjardins warning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss additional elements as mere 'generic computer components' without analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should not dismiss additional claim elements as mere generic computer components without considering whether such elements confer a technological improvement to a technical problem, especially for improvements to computer components or the computer system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether claimed computer/system elements meaningfully contribute to the technological improvement; Desjardins and other precedents show that elements previously characterized as generic may nonetheless be part of an improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification conclusory statements about improvement are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification explicitly sets forth an improvement but only in a conclusory manner (i.e., a bare assertion of an improvement without the detail necessary to be apparent to a person of ordinary skill in the art), the examiner should not determine that the claim improves technology or a technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for the substantive description enabling a POSITA to appreciate the improvement; mere assertions or boilerplate claims of improvement do not satisfy this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use related considerations (particular machine; mere instructions to apply) to assist improvement determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The improvement consideration overlaps with other § 101 considerations, specifically the particular machine consideration and the 'mere instructions to apply an exception' consideration; evaluation of those considerations may assist examiners in determining whether a claim satisfies the improvement consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference MPEP § 2106.05(b) and § 2106.05(f) when relevant to assess whether claimed elements provide an actual technological solution rather than mere instructions to implement an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One / Prong Two analysis — allow Prong Two to integrate exceptions into practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if Step 2A Prong One finds the claims recite an abstract idea (e.g., a mathematical concept), Step 2A Prong Two may determine that the specification identifies improvements and that the claims, taken as a whole, integrate the judicial exception into a practical application such that the claims are outside the enumerated judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claims, when read in light of the specification, integrate the exception into a practical application (as in Ex Parte Desjardins where claims addressing catastrophic forgetting were deemed to integrate the exception at Prong Two).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of claims that improve technology (non-exhaustive precedential list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that improve technology or a technical field and are not directed to a judicial exception include precedential examples such as Enfish (self-referential data structure), McRO (automatic lip synchronization and facial animation), Visual Memory (enhanced computer memory), Finjan (virus scanning improvements), SRI (network monitoring/suspicious activity detection), and Ex Parte Desjardins (ML training improvements and data-structure-like adjustments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these cases as illustrative examples of how claims can be found to be technological improvements; additional examples are provided in MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize machine-learning-specific improvements as technological improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: An improved way of training a machine learning model that protected the model’s knowledge about previous tasks while allowing it to effectively learn new tasks can show an improvement in computer functionality (e.g., overcoming 'catastrophic forgetting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex Parte Desjardins treated reduced storage, reduced system complexity, streamlining, and preservation of performance attributes across tasks as technological improvements disclosed in the specification and credited those benefits when evaluating eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to component/system performance via ML parameter adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements to computer component or system performance based upon adjustments to parameters of a machine learning model associated with tasks or workstreams may show an improvement in computer functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting adjustments in values to a plurality of performance parameters while preserving prior values (as in Desjardins) can reflect improvements tantamount to how the machine learning model itself would function in operation and therefore not be subsumed in an identified mathematical calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that recite a technological solution to a technological problem are 'more than apply it' instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that specify how interactions or components are manipulated to yield a desired result — i.e., recite a technological solution to a technological problem — have been found to be more than merely instructing to apply an abstract idea or to use a law of nature (DDR Holdings, BASCOM, Thales Visionix).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for claim limitations that recite how the technological result is achieved (specific configurations, manipulations, or methods) rather than mere high-level goals; such specific technological solutions may overcome the 'apply it' or 'mere instructions' rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider full claim scope under BRI when determining whether claim reflects improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation should be considered to determine if the claim reflects an improvement in technology or a technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on selected phrasing; consider how the claim limitations as a whole would be interpreted under BRI to assess whether they capture a particular solution or way of achieving a desired outcome rather than merely an idea or outcome.
